results.title: Spot pricing for GPU Servers – Documentation
highlights:
# Spot pricing for GPU Servers

July 6, 2026 · Announcement

We are introducing spot pricing for GPU Servers, giving you access to the same high-performance hardware at a reduced cost for workloads that can tolerate interruptions.

Spot pricing is now available for NVIDIA L40S and NVIDIA B200 plans, both offered at a discount compared to standard on-demand pricing. Spot instances are identical to their on-demand counterparts in terms of hardware specifications and performance — the difference is that they can be reclaimed when capacity is needed, with a 30-second graceful shutdown notice. See Pricing for details.

Spot GPU Servers are a good fit for:

- Batch inference and data processing pipelines.
- Model training jobs that support checkpointing.
- Development, experimentation, and testing.
- Any GPU workload that can be interrupted and resumed.

Storage and IP addresses are preserved if a spot instance is stopped, so you can pick up where you left off when capacity becomes available again.

results.title: AWS On-Demand GPU Prices Spike 20%, Spot Market Next — TechReaderDaily
highlights:
On July 1, 2026, Amazon Web Services raised the per-accelerator hourly price of its GPU instances by roughly 20 percent. The P6-B300, its top-tier Nvidia-powered instance family, now bills at $14.04 per accelerator-hour. The P6-B200 moved to $12.355. The P5, the prior generation, hit $5.191 in US regions. These are on-demand, no-commitment list prices, and they represent the second hike AWS has pushed through this year, following a 15 percent increase earlier in the spring, as The Next Web reported alongside the updated rate card.

The proximate cause is the memory supply chain. Tom's Hardware reported last October that AI data centers are consuming memory and storage at a pace that is outstripping legacy DRAM production capacity, and the situation has not eased. HBM3e stacks, the high-bandwidth memory that every H100, H200, and B300 depends on, remain tightly allocated. Add a helium shortage that Forbes detailed in April, which constrains the semiconductor fabrication equipment that depends on helium for cooling during lithography, and you have a supply-side vise that gives hyperscalers both the cover and the motive to raise prices. AWS did not blame the memory crunch in its customer notice. It did not need to. The invoice does the talking.

The price increase widens a gap that has been growing for eighteen months: the spread between what a hyperscaler charges for on-demand GPU compute and what a neocloud charges for a one-year reserved commitment. Chris Campbell, senior director of AI solutions and GPU-as-a-service at World Wide Technology, put the neocloud math on the record with CRN in June. A one-year deal for 1,000 Nvidia B300s at $5 per chip-hour comes to roughly $45 million. At the new AWS on-demand P6-B300 rate of $14.04 per accelerator-hour, the same thousand chips would cost $123 million over a year, before any reserved-instance discount. Even after the standard hyperscaler one-year commitment discount, the neocloud price per GPU-hour lands somewhere between 50 and 60 percent below the hyperscaler on-demand equivalent.

results.title: Rent per hour is not cost per token | Keftek
highlights:
## Two GPU generations moving apart

Amazon charges $98.84 an hour to reserve a Capacity Block of eight B200s, about $12.36 per GPU-hour, and says it moves that price on supply and demand. In our July 13 Vast.ai snapshot the B200 asking range rose to $7.25 to $9.92 an hour, up from about $5 a week earlier, while the upper end for last-generation H100 and H200 spot offers eased. Two GPU generations, moving apart.

It is tempting to read that as the shortage narrowing onto Blackwell. Be careful. These are asking-price ranges on one marketplace, and the snapshot merges board variants like H100 SXM and PCIe into a single range, so a move can reflect what is on offer rather than what is scarce. And hourly rent is not what a workload costs. A B200 rents for more than an H100 and can still produce a cheaper token, because throughput, batching, and memory fit decide cost per token, not the sticker on the hour.

So the honest read is narrow. Reserved rates are high across generations; one marketplace's Blackwell asks rose this week while its Hopper asks fell. For what to build on, the number that decides it is cost per token under comparable terms, not the hourly rate.

In the July 13 Vast.ai snapshot, B200 asks rose to $7.25–$9.92/hr from about $5 a week earlier while H100 and H200 upper ranges eased; these are marketplace asking prices, not cost per token.

results.title: Cloud GPU Capacity Up 20% at AWS: Engineers Adapt Now
highlights:
On July 1, 2026, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML prices by roughly 20% per accelerator-hour, its second hike in six months after a ~15% increase in January (Converge Digest). A reserved P6-B300 (Blackwell Ultra) now costs $14.04/hr. Cloud GPU capacity — the scarce fabric every foundation-model training and production inference run depends on — just got measurably more expensive for the platform teams that book it up to eight weeks ahead.

...

Capacity Blocks are AWS’s marketplace for guaranteed AI accelerator capacity, hosted in EC2 UltraClusters and reservable up to eight weeks in advance for windows of up to six months, in clusters of one to 64 instances (AWS). Unlike Reserved Instances, they demand no one- or three-year commitment — you pay the prevailing reservation fee upfront and get guaranteed, low-latency, high-throughput fabric for the window you booked. After July 1, 2026, the headline rates per accelerator moved decisively upward.

| Instance | Accelerator | New Rate (US) | Rate Outside US |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | Blackwell Ultra | $14.04/hr | $14.04/hr (ex-GovCloud) |
| P6-B200 | Blackwell | $12.355/hr | $12.355/hr |
| P5en | H200 (networked) | $6.865/hr | $6.241/hr |
| P5e | H200 | $5.97/hr | $5.97/hr |
| P5 | H100 | $5.191/hr | $4.72/hr |
| P4de | A100 | $2.214/hr | — |

The critical wrinkle: AWS bills the reservation fee upfront when you book, and OS charges separately during runtime, with prices “updated periodically based on supply and demand” (AWS). You pay the rate in force at purchase time even if the reserved window starts after a future increase. That clause turns pricing announcements into a procurement clock — every team with a training run landing in Q3 just had its budget recalculated. The P6e-GB200 (NVIDIA GB200 NVL72) and Trainium Trn2 instances are also supported, signaling that AWS is pricing the entire accelerated fleet on a dynamic, demand-revealing curve rather than a static rate card.

...

That model put on-demand AWS P6-B200 (Blackwell) at $12.36/GPU-hr and P5 (H100) at $12.29/GPU-hr, normalized per GPU from eight-GPU flagship instances — meaning the cheapest GPU-hour rarely wins, because the providers that discount compute often recover it on network line items that never appear on the headline rate card (HackerNoon) — a dynamic we examined in detail when cloud egress fees surpassed GPU compute costs for AI workloads. For platform teams, the implication is structural: any GPU procurement decision that quotes only dollars-per-GPU-hour is incomplete by design. A 20% capacity-block hike on compute, layered on a workload where egress is already a third of spend, compresses margins in a way no single line item reveals.

1. The $/TB/s band. On 2026-09-28 it runs $0.86–1.13, with B300 at $1.00. If serving demand deepens, the band should tighten and new generations enter inside it. If training demand tightens, Blackwell should move above it.
2. Term structure loads the short end. Inference buyers resist tenors beyond one year. The 1Y cell becomes the tenor where committed pricing concentrates.
3. The guaranteed–interruptible spread on older generations. On 2026-09-28: H100 Neocloud guaranteed $3.56, interruptible $2.16 (-39%); A100 $2.30 and $1.20 (-48%). A lasting narrowing on old generations would mean bursty serving demand is reaching down the ladder.
4. Old-generation floors hold. In power-market terms, depreciated chips are peakers (low carrying cost, dispatched into demand spikes) while new fleets are baseload needing committed offtake. A100 at $1.13/TB/s at 5.8 years is the floor holding. Watch it as Blackwell supply normalizes.
5. Utilization becomes the swing variable. Serving is diurnal, training is flat. Realized-vs-posted gaps widen for serving-heavy operators even where posted rates hold.
6. Contract quality shifts. Many short-tenor customers replace one five-year offtake: diversification up, committed coverage down. Underwriting moves from offtake credit toward market-rate reference.
7. The liquid watt-premium. On 2026-09-28, liquid-class Blackwell rents at $6.85–7.03 per kW-hr against $4.49–5.75 for air-cooled chips. As liquid-cooled halls build out, the gap should narrow. If the air band falls first, old-generation floors break from the facility side.

results.title: The Complete Guide to GPU Cloud Pricing in 2026: H100, H200, B200, and Beyond | nasscom | The Official Community of Indian IT Industry
highlights:
### NVIDIA H100: The Commodity Workhorse

Once the undisputed king of AI training, the Hopper-based H100 has officially become a highly accessible, cost-effective commodity in 2026.

- The Technical Reality: Equipped with 80GB of HBM3 memory, it remains incredibly potent for standard fine-tuning tasks and running mid-sized model inferences.
- Pricing Breakdown: On specialized clouds like RunPod or Lambda Labs, on-demand pricing has stabilized between $1.92 and $3.29 per GPU-hour. Meanwhile, if you look at secondary marketplaces or spot/preemptible instances, the floor drops to as low as $1.03 per hour. Compare this to AWS, where an equivalent H100 (p5 instance) hovers around $6.88 per hour, and Microsoft Azure, which pushes up to $12.29 per hour.

### NVIDIA H200: The Inference Sweet Spot

The H200 represents a mid-generation upgrade over the H100, but its impact on model deployment economics cannot be overstated.

- The Technical Reality: The H200 features a massive jump to 141GB of ultra-fast HBM3e memory and a 50% increase in memory bandwidth. Because LLM inference is highly "memory-bound" (meaning performance is throttled by how fast the chip can read data from its memory rather than raw calculation speeds), a single H200 can frequently replace multiple H100s by fitting massive parameter models onto fewer chips.
- Pricing Breakdown: On-demand rates on specialized networks sit comfortably at $3.31 to $4.54 per hour, presenting an unparalleled price-to-performance ratio for hosting internal production APIs.

### NVIDIA B200 (Blackwell): The High-Performance Powerhouse

NVIDIA’s Blackwell architecture has fully arrived, representing a historic paradigm shift in deep learning efficiency.

- The Technical Reality: Boasting 192GB of HBM3e memory and native FP4 precision capabilities, a single B200 chip delivers up to 2.3x the raw compute speed of an H100.
- Pricing Breakdown: This elite performance commands a launch premium. Specialized clouds rent out B200 instances for $4.95 to $7.15 per hour on-demand. If your enterprise scales out to the legacy hyperscalers, expect a massive price jump: AWS and Google Cloud demand between $14.24 and $16.11 per GPU-hour for B200 clusters.
